@@123970174 <h> Big Questions , Bold Answers <p> The typical college general education curriculum , fractured into discipline-based silos , often fails to engage students with the profound questions and pressing controversies that shape human life and society . Instead of equipping students to address the complexities of the modern world , these curricula isolate disciplinary knowledge , offering fragmented learning experiences . <p> To prepare students for the challenges of a globalized , rapidly changing world , higher education needs a transformative approach : an interdisciplinary curriculum that integrates insights from multiple fields and connects enduring questions with contemporary issues . Such a curriculum would prioritize intellectual exploration , critical thinking and ethical reasoning , enabling students to develop a holistic understanding of the world and their role within it . <h> Most Popular <p> Here are examples of courses that would form the foundation of this reimagined general education curriculum : <p> Intimacy and Caring in an Individualistic World <p> Modern societies prioritize autonomy and individual achievement , often at the expense of meaningful relationships and caregiving . This course explores how intimacy and care are shaped by cultural @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ philosophy and literature , students examine : <p> The historical evolution of intimacy and caregiving . <p> The impact of technologies like dating apps and social media on relationships . <p> Tensions between independence and interdependence . <p> Alternative models of community and caregiving , including nontraditional family structures . <p> Through case studies and creative projects , students critically analyze humanity 's impact on the natural world and envision sustainable futures . <p> These courses exemplify a reimagined general education curriculum that prioritizes interdisciplinarity and engagement with enduring questions and contemporary controversies . By integrating insights from multiple fields , this approach equips students with the intellectual tools , ethical frameworks and cultural understanding necessary to navigate a complex , interconnected world . <p> Far from being fragmented or superficial , this vision fosters critical thinking , creativity and a sense of responsibility -- qualities essential for addressing the challenges of the 21st century . Such a curriculum would not only transform higher education but also empower students to make meaningful contributions to society . <p> The concept of general education has undergone profound transformations over time , evolving @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , discipline-based model that defines much of modern higher education today . This shift reflects changes in societal priorities , economic structures and institutional organization , driven by industrialization , the rise of specialized disciplines and the demands of bureaucratic efficiency . <h> The Classical Liberal Arts Tradition <p> In its earliest incarnation , general education was synonymous with the classical liberal arts , rooted in the ancient Greek and Roman ideals of cultivating well-rounded citizens capable of reasoned thought , ethical action and civic engagement . The trivium ( grammar , rhetoric and logic ) and quadrivium ( arithmetic , geometry , music and astronomy ) formed the cornerstone of this education , emphasizing intellectual breadth and the interconnectivity of knowledge . <p> Education in this model aimed not at narrow vocational training but at developing individuals with the intellectual and moral virtues necessary for participation in public life . <p> The liberal arts tradition carried into the medieval period , where universities such as those in Bologna , Paris and Oxford continued to emphasize a unified curriculum that integrated theology , philosophy and natural sciences . Knowledge was @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that studying the natural and moral order led to greater understanding of divine and human truths . <h> The Impact of Industrialization <p> The Industrial Revolution brought profound changes to education , as the demands of an industrial economy emphasized practical skills and technical expertise . Universities increasingly adapted to meet these needs , shifting focus from general intellectual development to specialized training . <p> The classical liberal arts curriculum , viewed as less immediately applicable to the burgeoning industries of the time , began to wane in favor of education tailored to professions like engineering , business and medicine . <p> This period also saw the rise of research universities , particularly in Germany , which became influential models for institutions worldwide . These universities emphasized disciplinary specialization and the production of new knowledge over the teaching of a unified curriculum . Fields such as physics , chemistry and economics emerged as distinct disciplines , each with its own methods , goals and professional organizations . <p> In the United States , the Morrill Land-Grant Acts of 1862 and 1890 further accelerated this shift by providing federal funding for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ While many land-grant colleges incorporated elements of the liberal arts , their primary mission was to prepare students for the practical demands of industrial and agricultural professions . This marked a turning point , as higher education increasingly prioritized specialization and technical training over the integrative aims of the liberal arts tradition . <h> The Rise of Specialized Disciplines <p> The late 19th and early 20th centuries solidified the dominance of disciplinary specialization . Advances in science and technology created a demand for experts who could push the boundaries of knowledge within narrowly defined fields . This era saw the proliferation of academic departments , each dedicated to a specific discipline , as universities reorganized themselves to reflect the segmented nature of modern knowledge . <p> Faculty members were increasingly trained as specialists in doctoral programs that emphasized deep expertise in a single area of study , often at the expense of broader intellectual engagement . <p> As disciplines solidified , so too did their accompanying professional associations , journals and conferences , creating self-contained intellectual ecosystems . This further entrenched the idea that expertise resided within narrowly defined boundaries @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and less valued . <h> Bureaucratic Organization and Efficiency <p> The rise of bureaucratic organization in the 20th century further fragmented the concept of general education . Universities , now large and complex institutions , adopted hierarchical structures to manage their growing enrollments and diverse academic offerings . General education , once a cohesive curriculum designed to provide a shared foundation , became a collection of distribution requirements , with students selecting courses from a menu of options across disparate departments . <p> This approach , while offering flexibility , often resulted in a fragmented educational experience . Students fulfilled general education requirements without encountering a unifying vision or coherent intellectual framework . Knowledge became compartmentalized , with little emphasis on the connections between disciplines or the broader questions that transcend individual fields of study . <p> Bureaucratic pressures also emphasized efficiency and standardization , which worked against the integrative aims of general education . The need to streamline curricula to accommodate larger student bodies led to the erosion of interdisciplinary courses , which are often more resource-intensive to design and teach . In this environment , the focus shifted @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , rather than holistic intellectual development . <h> The Current Landscape <p> Today 's general education curricula reflect this history of fragmentation . While most institutions still require students to complete courses across a range of disciplines , these requirements are often treated as boxes to be checked rather than as part of a coherent intellectual journey . Students frequently experience general education as a series of disconnected courses , lacking the integrative vision necessary to address the complex , interconnected challenges of the modern world . <p> Efforts to revive the interdisciplinary spirit of the classical liberal arts tradition face significant structural and cultural barriers . However , as global challenges such as climate change , inequality and technological disruption demand holistic and integrative thinking , there is a growing recognition of the need to rethink the general education curriculum . By drawing on the strengths of both the liberal arts tradition and modern disciplinary expertise , institutions have the opportunity to create a transformative educational model that equips students to engage with enduring questions and contemporary controversies . <h> Climate Change <p> Climate change illustrates the necessity of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ requiring expertise in climatology , environmental science and renewable energy , science alone can not resolve the crisis . Understanding the economic incentives driving fossil fuel consumption , political resistance to regulatory measures and the social impacts of environmental degradation necessitates perspectives from economics , political science and sociology . <p> Philosophy and ethics add depth to debates about intergenerational justice and the moral responsibilities of individuals , corporations and nations . Meanwhile , art and literature amplify awareness by using narratives and imagery to make the abstract and often overwhelming reality of climate change more tangible and emotionally compelling . <h> Global Inequality <p> Addressing global inequality also demands a cross-disciplinary approach . Economic disparities are shaped not only by market forces but also by historical legacies of colonialism , systemic racism and unequal access to education and health care . Tackling these inequities requires the integration of history , sociology , economics and political science . <p> Philosophers and ethicists grapple with moral dilemmas such as algorithmic bias and the rights of autonomous machines . Sociologists study automation 's effects on employment and inequality , while political scientists @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Legal scholars tackle intellectual property rights and data privacy , and psychologists examine how digital technologies impact mental health and behavior . <h> Public Health Crises <p> The COVID-19 pandemic underscored the need for integrated thinking in public health . Combating the virus required scientific expertise from epidemiologists and virologists , but effective management also depended on insights from social scientists , who assessed how misinformation spread , and economists , who analyzed the financial impacts of lockdowns . Political scientists evaluated policy responses , while historians contextualized the crisis by drawing parallels with past pandemics . <p> Ethicists contributed by addressing vaccine distribution and balancing individual freedoms with public safety , and communication specialists played a vital role in crafting effective public health messages . This interdisciplinary collaboration proved crucial in saving lives and mitigating the pandemic 's global impact . <h> Social and Political Polarization <p> The growing polarization within societies also demands contributions from multiple disciplines . Political scientists analyze the structures and systems that deepen partisan divides , while psychologists examine cognitive biases that reinforce polarization . Sociologists explore the role of social media in creating @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <h> Global Migration <p> Migration , driven by economic opportunity , political conflict and environmental crises , requires nuanced , interdisciplinary understanding . Anthropology and sociology illuminate the lived experiences of migrants , while political science examines policies governing borders and citizenship . Economics evaluates migration 's impact on labor markets and development and history contextualizes migration patterns within broader trends of globalization and colonialism . <p> Art and literature capture the human dimension of displacement , offering narratives that challenge stereotypes and build empathy . Ethical and legal perspectives address the rights of refugees and the responsibilities of host nations , revealing the interconnected causes and consequences of migration . <h> The Role of Higher Education <p> Higher education plays a critical role in fostering interdisciplinary thinking . While traditional academic boundaries deepen expertise , they must be complemented by programs that encourage students to connect knowledge across fields . Interdisciplinary courses can address contemporary challenges by combining diverse perspectives . For example , a general education course on climate change could integrate environmental science , public policy and ethics , while one on global migration might draw @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ interdisciplinary knowledge , colleges and universities can prepare students to confront 21st-century challenges with creativity , adaptability and a holistic perspective . Only by transcending traditional academic boundaries can we hope to address the profound and interconnected issues that define our time . <p> Interdisciplinary courses addressing enduring questions and contemporary controversies have the potential to transform higher education . By integrating insights from multiple fields , these courses provide students with the analytical tools and ethical frameworks essential for navigating an increasingly complex , interconnected world . Despite their value , however , implementing such courses faces significant challenges within the traditional structures of higher education . Overcoming these barriers requires targeted reforms and innovative strategies . <p> The structural organization of graduate programs further entrenches disciplinary silos . Departments operate as self-contained units , fostering limited interaction across fields and immersing students in the methodologies and literature of their discipline . Interdisciplinary opportunities , when available , are often undervalued or seen as peripheral , reinforcing the perception that interdisciplinarity is less rigorous than traditional scholarship . <p> Another significant issue is the lack of pedagogical training in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ supporting single-discipline courses , providing minimal exposure to course design , let alone the development of interdisciplinary classes . Without deliberate preparation , many future educators lack the skills and confidence to create and teach courses that address broad questions and integrate diverse perspectives . <p> Academic incentive structures also discourage interdisciplinary teaching . Hiring and tenure processes emphasize research output and disciplinary specialization over teaching innovation . Graduate students internalize these priorities early , focusing on producing publishable research rather than exploring creative approaches to education . Faculty who devote time to interdisciplinary course design frequently find their efforts undervalued , as such work is rarely recognized as a significant academic contribution . <p> Cultural norms within academia exacerbate these challenges . Interdisciplinary work is often perceived as less rigorous or legitimate than traditional disciplinary scholarship , discouraging graduate students and faculty from pursuing it . As a result , courses designed to engage students with big questions and contemporary controversies are often sidelined before they are conceptualized . <p> Curriculum constraints further hinder interdisciplinary course development . General education requirements are often rigid , emphasizing breadth by requiring @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but offering little room for integration . Students , as a result , encounter fragmented knowledge instead of cohesive interdisciplinary perspectives . Accreditation standards and degree pathways , which emphasize traditional disciplinary frameworks , further restrict flexibility . <p> Resource limitations also present significant challenges , especially for smaller institutions or underfunded departments . Designing and delivering interdisciplinary courses requires additional resources , including support for team teaching , curriculum development and administrative coordination . Specialized faculty training and investments in collaborative tools may also be necessary , further straining budgets . <p> Student perceptions add another layer of difficulty . Influenced by societal and parental pressures , many students prioritize courses they believe will directly advance their career goals . Interdisciplinary courses , which emphasize broad conceptual thinking over immediate vocational skills , are often misunderstood as impractical . This misconception can lead to lower enrollment and reduced institutional support for such offerings . <p> Addressing these barriers requires bold , systemic changes . By fostering collaboration , revising curricular structures and realigning incentive systems , institutions can create interdisciplinary courses that prepare students to confront the complexities of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ perspective . <p> To address these challenges , campuses must adopt bold and innovative strategies that prioritize interdisciplinary learning as a core component of the general education curriculum . Encouraging faculty collaboration is a key first step . Institutions can incentivize team teaching and interdisciplinary course development through grants , course release time and shared teaching credits . <p> Professional development programs can equip faculty with the skills and confidence to teach across disciplines , fostering a culture of collaboration that breaks down departmental silos . <p> Revising curriculum structures is also essential . Institutions should build flexibility into general education requirements , allowing for thematic tracks or clusters that address broad societal challenges . For instance , students could choose interdisciplinary pathways focused on sustainability , justice or global citizenship , integrating courses from multiple fields into cohesive learning experiences . <p> Realigning incentive systems is equally critical . Promotion and tenure policies must value teaching innovation and interdisciplinary scholarship on par with traditional research output . Offering grants , awards and public recognition for faculty who lead interdisciplinary initiatives would further encourage collaboration and creativity . <p> Leveraging @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Cross-departmental collaborations enable institutions to pool expertise and funding , while partnerships with external organizations , such as nonprofits or industries , provide real-world applications for interdisciplinary courses . For example , a course on environmental sustainability could involve collaboration with local conservation groups , giving students practical experience alongside academic learning . <p> Engaging students and stakeholders is another vital strategy . Institutions must clearly communicate the value of interdisciplinary courses , highlighting their relevance to career preparation and personal development . Showcasing how these courses foster critical thinking , adaptability and problem-solving skills can build student interest and support . Involving students in shaping the curriculum through surveys , focus groups or pilot programs ensures that courses resonate with their interests and aspirations . <p> Pilot programs and assessment initiatives can pave the way for broader adoption of interdisciplinary courses . Small-scale experiments allow institutions to refine course designs and demonstrate their value to students and faculty . Data on student outcomes and satisfaction can build momentum and secure funding for expansion . <p> Interdisciplinary courses that tackle enduring questions and contemporary controversies are not merely valuable -- @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the complexities of today 's world . The challenges we face today -- climate change , inequality , technological disruption and social fragmentation -- demand integrative thinking , ethical reasoning and the ability to draw connections across disciplines . A general education curriculum that embraces these imperatives can serve as a transformative force , equipping students with the intellectual tools and moral compass necessary to lead and innovate in uncertain times . <p> Reimagining general education is not just about addressing academic silos ; it is about empowering a new generation of thinkers , leaders and citizens . Such a curriculum would cultivate critical thinking , creativity and a deep sense of social responsibility . Students would emerge from these courses not as specialists in their chosen fields but as individuals capable of seeing the bigger picture -- connecting knowledge to action , ideas to solutions and personal growth to collective progress . <p> This is a call to action for colleges and universities to confront the structural , cultural and pedagogical barriers that inhibit interdisciplinary learning . @@124073564 <h> Cascadia subduction zone earthquake could be even worse than feared <p> A once-every-500-years earthquake in the Pacific Northwest could shake for five minutes and cause 100-foot tsunami waves . New research says that would be just the start of the horrors . <p> Researchers conduct shallow sediment sampling in the Salmon River estuary in Oregon in 2023 . They are using gouge corers and GPS surveying equipment to document stratigraphy and land-level changes following past earthquakes and tsunamis.Mike Priddy <p> When an earthquake rips along the Cascadia Subduction Zone fault , much of the U.S. west coast could shake violently for five minutes , and tsunami waves as tall as 100 feet could barrel toward shore . But that 's just the start of the expected horrors . <p> Even if coastal towns in Northern California , Oregon and Washington withstand that seismic onslaught , new research suggests floodwaters could seep into many of these vulnerable communities for good . That 's because entire coastal shorelines are expected to drop by as much as 6 ? feet when the earthquake strikes , according to new research , published Monday @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ PNAS ) . <p> Researchers analyzed seismic and flood modeling to produce some of the most detailed estimates of how the Cascadia earthquake would drop -- or subside -- coastal shorelines and found that it could affect more than double the number of people , structures and roads currently at risk . The effect will also worsen over time , as intensifying climate change raises sea levels further . <p> " This lesser talked about hazard is going to persist for decades or centuries after the earthquake , " said Tina Dura , the study 's lead author . " The tsunami will come in and wash away and it 's going to have big impacts , do n't get me wrong , but the lasting change of the frequency of flooding ... that 's going to have to be dealt with . " <p> A team operates a vibracore rig in Siletz Bay , Ore. , to collect deep sediment cores for tsunami deposit and paleoseismic analysis in 2022 . The cores will help researchers better understand the history of past great earthquakes along the Cascadia subduction zone.Tina Dura @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ earthquakes immediately dropped the land level and turned dry ground into tidal mudflats in estuaries along the Pacific Northwest . <p> " That 's going to happen again and we 've built up a lot of those areas , " said Dura , who is an assistant professor of geosciences at Virginia Tech University . " That 's how we have ports there ... and that 's where we built towns , and all that area is gon na drop down maybe over a meter , up to two meters . " <p> The Cascadia Subduction Zone fault , which runs offshore along North America 's west coast from Northern California to northern Vancouver Island , represents a looming threat . The fault has the capability to produce a magnitude-9.0 earthquake , and a large temblor is expected there at least once every 450-500 years , on average . The last of those major quakes occurred in 1700 . <p> The National Seismic Hazard Model suggests there is a 15% chance a magnitude-8.0 earthquake or stronger will rupture along the zone 's margin within the next 50 years . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ precipitate the worst natural disaster in the nation 's history . A 2022 state and federal planning exercise for a Cascadia earthquake predicted about 14,000 fatalities , more than 100,000 injuries and the collapse of about 620,000 buildings in the Pacific Northwest , including 100 hospitals and 2,000 schools . <p> The new research suggests that coastal planners must seriously reckon not only for the threat of intense shaking and tsunami waves , but also for the long-term reshaping and rapid sinking of the coastline itself . <p> " There 's the flood itself and then there 's the basically permanent change to land level at the coast and that has a big impact for what those communities have to plan for , " said Harold Tobin , the director of the Pacific Northwest Seismic Network and a professor at the University of Washington , who was not involved in the new research . " Where are you going to put your school or hospital ? Where are you going to build your transportation network ? I think it 's important to take the long view . " <p> After @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of towns along the Pacific Northwest coastline , such as Seaside , Oregon ; Westport , Washington ; and Aberdeen , Washington , would be expected to flood at least once every 100 years , if not more often . <p> The study also points out that sea level rise is accelerating as climate change intensifies , and the effects of post-earthquake flooding could worsen in the future . <p> A field team treks across the Salmon River estuary in Oregon carrying coring and surveying equipment to their next sampling site in 2023 . Researchers mapped and sampled sediment deposits to reconstruct the geologic history of earthquake-driven subsidence.Mike Priddy <p> Where you live could determine how dramatic sea level rise appears , and how it affects the coastline . <p> While land in some regions of the U.S. , like the Chesapeake Bay in Virginia , is slowly sinking in a process called subsidence , parts of the Pacific Northwest have been rising because of continental uplift . That rise in land level has offset some of the sea level rise to date . <p> The uplift is the result @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Cascadia subduction zone offshore . At the subduction zone , the Juan de Fuca plate is being forced beneath the continental North American plate . This causes the North American plate to bow upward slightly , pushing the land level higher . <p> Right now , the subduction zone fault is quiet and building stress . When the fault ruptures , the bowing of the plate will release and cause a rapid subsidence of the land level , essentially erasing centuries of uplift in an instant . <p> " That happens in minutes , and it can be on the order of meters , " Dura said . " The land persists down , and that can be for , like I said , decades and centuries . And so any areas that are kind of on the cusp of the floodplain are now in it . "

It provides biscuits and baked snacks , including cookies , crackers , salted snacks , snack bars , and cakes and pastries ; chocolates ; and gums and candies , as well as various cheese and grocery , and powdered beverage products . The company 's brand portfolio includes Oreo , Ritz , LU , CLIF Bar , and Tate 's Bake Shop biscuits and baked snacks , as well as Cadbury Dairy Milk , Milka , and Toblerone chocolate . It serves supermarket chains , wholesalers , supercenters , club stores , mass merchandisers , distributors , convenience stores , gasoline stations , drug stores , value stores , and other retail food outlets through direct store delivery , company-owned and satellite warehouses , distribution centers , third party distributors , and other facilities , as well as through independent sales offices and agents . The company also sells products directly to businesses and consumers through e-retail platforms , retailer digital platforms , as well as through its direct-to-consumer websites and social media platforms . Mondelez International , Inc. was formerly known as Kraft Foods Inc. and changed its name to Mondelez International , Inc. in October 2012 . @@124137561 <h> Spring allergies have returned <h> Here 's how to check pollen levels and keep from sneezing <h> KENYA HUNTER <h> The Associated Press <p> ATLANTA -- Allergy season can be miserable for tens of millions of Americans when trees , grass and other pollens cause runny noses , itchy eyes , coughing and sneezing . <p> Where you live , what you 're allergic to and your lifestyle can make a big difference when it comes to the severity of your allergies . <p> Experts say climate change is leading to longer and more intense allergy seasons , but also point out that treatments for seasonal allergies have become more effective over the last decade . <p> Here are some tips from experts to keep allergy symptoms at bay -- maybe even enough to allow you to enjoy the outdoors . <p> Where are pollen levels the worst this year ? <p> The Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America issues an annual ranking of the most challenging cities to live in if you have allergies , based on over-the-counter medicine use , pollen counts and the number of available @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cities are : Wichita , Kansas ; New Orleans ; Oklahoma City ; Tulsa , Oklahoma ; and Memphis . <p> Which pollens cause allergies ? <p> There are three main types of pollen . Earlier in the spring , tree pollen is the main culprit . After that grasses pollinate , followed by weeds in the late summer and early fall . <p> Some of the most common tree pollens that cause allergies include birch , cedar , cottonwood , maple , elm , oak and walnut , according to the Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America . Grasses that cause symptoms include Bermuda , Johnson , rye and Kentucky bluegrass . <p> How do I track pollen levels ? <p> Pollen trackers can help you decide when to go outside . The American Academy of Allergy Asthma and Immunology tracks levels through a network of counting stations across the U.S. Counts are available at its website and via email . <p> Limit your exposure to pollens <p> The best and first step to controlling allergies is avoiding exposure . <p> Keep the windows in your car and your @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> If you go outside , wearing long sleeves can keep pollen off your skin to help ward off allergic reactions , said Dr. James Baker , an allergist at the University of Michigan . It also provides some sun protection , he added . <p> When you get home , change your clothes and shower daily to ensure all the pollen is off of you -- including your hair . If you ca n't wash your hair every day , try covering it when you go outside with a hat or scarf . <p> Do n't get in the bed with your outside clothes on , because the pollen will follow . <p> It 's also useful to rinse your eyes and nose with saline to remove any pollen , experts said . And the same masks that got us through the pandemic can protect you from allergies -- though they wo n't help with eye symptoms . <p> How to relieve allergy symptoms <p> Over-the-counter nasal sprays are among the most effective treatments for seasonal allergies , experts said . <p> But the vast majority of patients use @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Dr. Kathleen Mays , an allergist at Augusta University in Georgia . She suggested angling the nozzle outward toward your ear rather than sticking it straight up your nose . <p> Over-the-counter allergy pills like Claritin , Allegra and Zyrtec are helpful , but may not be as effective as quickly since they 're taken by mouth , experts said . <p> Experts also said that if your allergy symptoms are impacting your quality of life , like causing you to lose sleep or a lack focus at work or school , it might be time to consider an allergist appointment for immunotherapies . <p> Some remedies for allergy relief that have been circulating on social media or suggested by celebrities -- like incorporating local honey into your diet to expose yourself to pollen -- have been debunked . <p> Dr. Shayam Joshi , an allergist at Oregon Health and Science University , said that 's because the flowers that bees pollinate typically do n't contain the airborne pollen that causes allergy symptoms . <p> Is allergy season changing ? <p> With climate change , winters are milder and growing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ pollen to stay in the air , resulting in longer and more severe allergy seasons . <p> In many areas across the country , pollen counts have broken decades of records . In late March , the Atlanta Allergy and Asthma Center measured a pollen count of over 14,000 grains per cubic meter , which is considered extremely high .

( Paul Sancya/The Associated Press ) <p> Opinion editor 's note:Strib Voices publishes a mix of guest commentaries online and in print each day . To contribute , click here . <p> *** <p> I first met Dane Chapin , a San Diego-area entrepreneur , in 2012 , when he gave me a ride in his Prius and told me I was dead wrong about climate change . We 've been close friends ever since . Sometimes he 's to my left politically , sometimes to my right . I 've always admired his curiosity , optimism and independent thinking , especially when we disagree -- as we did over his vote for Donald Trump in the last election . <p> One hundred days into this administration , Dane is n't happy . " With Trump I thought , maybe , there might be a method to the madness , " he told me on Saturday . " I 'm @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " <p> To hear from Dane now is particularly valuable for the insight he offers as to why a crucial constituency -- the business-minded but non-MAGA side of Trump 's base -- is beginning to sour on the president . It 's not about deportations , foreign aid , federal funding of universities or any of the issues that animate Trump 's usual critics . It 's about the tariffs . <p> " I 'm being forced into survival mode regarding my business and our 80 employees , who I care for like a family , " Dane told me . " I have bigger things to worry about than what 's going on with Harvard . " <p> Dane 's principal business , which his family started more than 30 years ago , is USAopoly , or " the Op " for short . It makes themed versions of board games like Monopoly and Clue , and brings new ones to market , like a family party game called Tapple . His employees , he said , have excellent benefits and salaries ranging from the high five figures on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ about 2,000 game ideas a year . Five or six make it to production . <p> A few years ago Dane tried to start a separate business with actor Scott Eastwood , called Made Here , which focused on products manufactured in the United States . Great concept , but it did n't pan out : " Americans love low prices more than they loathe a ' Made in China ' sticker , " Dane concluded . <p> As for the Op , roughly three-quarters of its games are made in China , with the rest made in the United States . He recognizes that , logistically , it would make greater sense to produce them closer to his primary market . <p> But that 's not the way this market works . China , he said , has " a highly developed supply chain that allows America to enjoy a wide range of quality toys and games at very affordable prices . " If he had to make all his products domestically , the retail prices for most of his games would rise to about $35 to $40 , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ market at this price , " he said , and he would also have to " dramatically shrink " his workforce . As for moving production to countries like India or Vietnam , it would take years . With no transition time , Trump 's tariffs have " the potential of obliterating the toy business . " <p> That 's the state of emergency that 's unfolding across his industry and beyond . In mid-March , Dane gave the green light for 15 containers of goods to be shipped from China . That was when the tariff rate was 20% . Before the goods could arrive in Vancouver for shipment to Indianapolis , the tariff rate had risen to 145% , potentially costing the company an additional $920,000 . <p> " These goods might now make a round trip to China to allow us to avoid the 145% tariff until the more permanent , and lower , tariff is decided on , " Dane explained . The tsunami of economic consequences is moving fast . He has put all China-based production on hold . " There is a very narrow @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ time for holiday shopping " -- by which he means Christmas . " Layoffs at many companies are already happening , " he added . " We are doing more of running a daily fire drill than running our business . " <p> What does Dane think of the Trump administration 's overall trade policy ? He does n't object to taking a harder line on China . But he 's offended that the president is making tariff exceptions for big tech companies but not for the smaller American businesses that the administration is supposed to champion . <p> " Apple has more than $60 billion in net cash in the bank and a market cap that is 231 times larger than the market cap of the two biggest U.S. toy companies combined , " he noted . " The toy industry is a blip economically , yet we have been put in deep peril by the chaotic and random execution of trade policy . " <p> Does all this mean that he now wishes he 'd voted for Kamala Harris ? Not at all . Trump , he says @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a president , Biden , who was plainly deceiving the country about his mental health , and a **26;907;TOOLONG candidate , Harris , who comes from the anti-business progressive wing of California politics that is ruining the state . " <p> " I do n't regret my vote , given the choices , " he added . " I do regret current trade policy . " <p> Certain readers of this column may be tempted to condemn Dane for caring more about the bottom line than the good of the country , as they see it . That strikes me as morally and politically obtuse . <p> Morally , because Dane 's focus on the bottom line translates directly to the livelihoods of 80 employees and the well-being of their families -- a greater good , in my book , than simply screaming about Trump 's awfulness . Politically , because Trump 's calamitous management of the economy should n't be an occasion to scold disaffected Trump voters . It 's a chance for a moderate , enterprising , business-friendly Democrat to win them over . " A drop of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ catches more flies than a gallon of gall . " <p> One additional point in the spirit of friendship : The tariffs Dane and so many others now suffer from were loudly trumpeted by the president during the campaign . The capricious and heavy-handed way in which they 've been imposed is of a piece with Trump 's capricious and heavy-handed character . And the contempt for legality , procedure , consultation and fairness that lies at the root of the current economic chaos is no surprise from a president who seems to think he can govern via an endless succession of executive orders and social media posts . <p> Voters who thought they could afford to be indifferent to the president 's indecencies , personal and political , should draw the lesson : If you let a pirate loose , do n't be surprised when he takes your ship .

The fire would eventually engulf around 700 acres . <p> They paid particular attention to how fast the fire was spreading , where it was gaining ground and how hot it was . <p> Prescribed burns are fires that are intentionally set to manage ecosystems that need periodic fires to stay healthy . @@124158463 <h> Loading .... <p> Concerns that the arsenic in brown rice can harm you are overblown . But pregnant women and toddlers should take extra precautions . Sung Min/Shutterstock <p> Which is healthiest : Brown or white rice ? <p> Nutrition experts have long urged people to choose brown rice whenever possible . One cup of brown rice has nearly six times the amount of fiber as white rice , as well as higher levels of magnesium , potassium , iron and B vitamins . Many studies have found that eating fiber-rich foods like brown rice and other whole grains is associated with a lower risk of developing heart disease , Type 2 diabetes , obesity and some cancers . <p> But in recent years , brown rice 's stellar reputation has been questioned . Some health and social media influencers have even discouraged people from eating it , saying brown rice should be avoided because it contains arsenic , a heavy metallinked to cancer , neurological problems and other health issues . <p> Health experts , however , say that concerns about arsenic in brown rice are mostly overstated @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ average levels of arsenic in both brown rice and white rice are low enough that you would have to eat excessive amounts to be at risk of developing health problems . Experts contend that the nutritional benefits of brown rice outweigh any concerns about arsenic when rice is part of a wide-ranging diet . <h> Related <p> A caveat is that some groups , such as infants and toddlers , may be more vulnerable to the harmful effects of arsenic . If you want to be cautious and limit your or your child 's exposure , there are things you can do , such as eating a variety of grains or cooking rice in a way that removes arsenic . <p> Why is there arsenic in rice ? <p> Advertisement <p> White rice and brown rice have a lot in common . In fact , white rice starts out as brown rice . The main difference between the two is how they are processed . <p> Brown rice is a whole grain that contains three key components . It has a fiber-rich outer layer called the bran , as well @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ healthy fats , antioxidants and vitamins . There is also a starchy middle layer called the endosperm , which contains simple carbohydrates as well as some protein and nutrients . <p> White rice is made by stripping brown rice of its bran and germ , leaving behind the starchy endosperm . This is why brown rice is more nutritious : It 's a whole grain that maintains all its fiber and nutrient-rich components . <p> But this can also be a downside . Rice is typically grown in flooded fields called rice paddies . When the soil is submerged underwater , arsenic in the ground becomes soluble and the plant 's roots can mistake the arsenic for nutrients and absorb it , said Andrew Meharg , the chair of plant and soil science at Queen 's University Belfast in Northern Ireland . <p> Because brown rice is converted to white rice by removing some of its components , white rice generally ends up containing about half as much arsenic as brown rice , said Meharg , who has studied arsenic contamination in rice for 25 years . <p> But the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ soil , the type of rice and how it 's cultivated . Some research suggests that climate change could also be causing higher levels of arsenic in rice . <p> Advertisement <p> How much arsenic is in rice ? <p> One recent study by researchers at Michigan State University looked at the average levels of inorganic arsenic in white and brown rice sold in the United States . It found that brown rice on average contained arsenic at levels around 138 parts per billion . The average levels in white rice were around 93 parts per billion . <p> Both averages are below the safety standards set by the World Health Organization . The agency says that " to protect consumers from excessive exposure , " arsenic levels in brown rice should not exceed a " maximum " of 350 parts per billion . <p> The Food and Drug Administration has n't issued any guidance on arsenic in rice and safe levels of consumption . But the agency regulates bottled water at 10 parts per billion and rice cereal for infants at 100 parts per billion . <p> How much @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the lead author of the Michigan State study and a postdoctoral research associate at the university , said the average American adult would need to eat more than three servings of brown rice -- one-and-a-half cups -- " every day for years " to be at an increased risk of developing health problems from the arsenic in rice . <p> Advertisement <p> " It 's not necessarily a reason to select white rice over brown rice at Chipotle when you 're an adult , " Scott said . <p> Beth Czerwony , a registered dietitian with the Cleveland Clinic 's Center for Human Nutrition , said that for adults , brown rice is so nutritious that you should n't be discouraged from eating it . <p> " For the general public , there 's really no reason to be worried , even for people who eat brown rice every day , " she added . <p> Should parents worry about arsenic in rice ? <p> More caution is warranted , however , for infants , toddlers and pregnant people . That 's because developing brains and nervous systems are more @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ toxins . Rice is a major ingredient in many infant foods -- such as infant cereals -- and it 's typically a first food for many children . <p> " They 're vulnerable . They 're developing , their cells are growing , organs forming , " said Margaret Karagas , a professor and chair of the department of epidemiology at the Geisel School of Medicine at Dartmouth College . " That is a sensitive period to environmental toxicants . " <p> Advertisement <p> If you 're pregnant , or you have an infant or toddler , consider a more diverse diet . <p> The American Academy of Pediatrics says that rice cereal does not need to be your infant 's first food . You can give them things like mashed or pureed avocado , bananas , butternut squash , sweet potatoes , beans or lentils . <p> If your child likes rice , you could give them a variety of other whole grains , such as oats , barley , quinoa and farro , which all have less arsenic than rice . The academy says you should try to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of processed toddler foods that use rice syrup as a sweetener . <p> One expert , Marie Muehe , an assistant professor at the Helmholtz Center for Environmental Research , has two children who are 3 and 5 years old . She said that when her children were younger , she cooked with rice " once a week , not more , " and then used other grains such as wheat and barley . <p> " It 's easy to implement , actually , " she said . " There just needs to be awareness . " <p> Can you reduce the amount of arsenic in rice ? <p> Advertisement <p> You could also reduce the amount of arsenic in your rice by using the following cooking method : <p> -- Soak the rice for 30 minutes then rinse thoroughly . Strain it . <p> -- Cook the rice in a fresh pot of boiling water , in the same way you 'd cook pasta , using at least a four-to-one ratio of water to rice . <p> -- Once the rice is cooked , strain it and discard the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ be in the excess water , " said Meharg , from Queen 's University Belfast . " Not all of it . But a lot of it . " <p> If you 're pressed for time , you could parboil the rice , instead of soaking it.In a study published in 2021 , researchers parboiled rice for five minutes and then finished cooking the grain in a fresh pot of water . @@124159466 <h> Since 2007 , European industry has reduced its emissions of harmful pollutants into the air and water by between 40% and 75% , according to data from the European Environment Agency . The EU now wants to go further towards a clean and competitive industry . <p> It is estimated that the 50,000 largest installations in the EU still account for around 40% of greenhouse gas emissions and are responsible for 20% of all air and water pollutants . <p> These pollutants have a significant impact on human health and the environment : <p> SOx , heavy metals and ammonia are harmful to crops , wildlife and humans . <p> Greenhouse gases cause climate change and reduce air quality . <p> A sharp fall in emissions <p> Pollution caused by industrial emissions accounts for billions of euros in costs and hundreds of thousands of premature deaths in the EU every year . <p> However , according to the European Environment Agency , environmental and health costs of European industry have decreased by a third from 2012 to 2021 . The EEA says the EU energy sector has accounted for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the same study , this is mainly due to the adoption of new techniques and the shift to renewables and less polluting fuels , both changes being largely as a result of EU action . <p> The European Union recently revised its Industrial Emissions Directive ( IED 2.0 ) , its main tool for taking action on pollution coming from the continent 's largest factories and farms . <p> Under this directive , installations have been required to comply with the environmental performance associated with the best available techniques ( BAT ) in their sector . A growing number of governments in the world are now seeking to adopt the same approach . <p> These performances are decided during the ' Sevilla process ' , a collaborative governance model involving industry , EU Member States and civil society , which takes place at the Joint European Research Centre ( JRC ) in Seville . <p> Currently , around 80% of industrial sites comply with the highest permitted emission limit values . Under the IED 2.0 directive , the competent authorities in the Member States will be required to use more @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Available Techniques are set to also take into account more explicitly the human health and climate protection of installations . <p> Decarbonisation efforts <p> The new rules aim to achieve a further 40% reduction in the main atmospheric pollutants by 2050 . One aim is to confirm the trend observed in recent decades : EU industry has grown while reducing its impact on the environment , a process known as ' decoupling ' . <p> Another important aspect of the revised directive is to support innovation and guide investment to boost Europe 's green competitiveness on the basis of the Clean Industrial Deal recently presented by the European Commission . <p> In Seville , a new Innovation Centre for Industrial Transformation and Emissions ( INCITE ) has been set up to identify and characterise the most promising technologies for achieving circular economy and carbon neutrality . <p> The European Union 's objectives are to reach carbon neutrality and zero pollution by 2050 . A new portal makes it possible to track changes in the levels of various pollutants in the different regions of Europe . <p> The European Environment Agency @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of the 33 actions announced in the 2021 ' zero pollution ' action plan , but that further efforts are still needed to achieve the objectives .

@@124160675 <h> Rejuvenating the lake is critical for Kerala , but it is easier said than done <p> A view of houseboats on Vembanad Lake in Alappuzha . Photo Credit : The Hindu <p> Vembanad , the longest lake in India and the largest in Kerala , is gasping for breath . The 96.5 km-long water body spans the districts of Alappuzha , Kottayam , and Ernakulam and forms part of the Vembanad-Kol wetland system , a Ramsar site . Six major rivers drain into the lake , which accounts for around 30% of the State 's total surface water resource . <p> Over the past century , the lake has shrunk significantly due to human-induced interventions , land reclamation , and natural sedimentation , according to experts . Though vital to the region 's ecology and agriculture , it faces severe threats from pollution , eutrophication , unsustainable agricultural practices , and invasive weed proliferation . <p> A few years ago , a study by the Kerala University of Fisheries and Ocean Studies revealed alarming levels of plastic waste , silt , and other sediments in the lake . According @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Vembanad Lake Rejuvenation Project , an ambitious joint effort of the Alappuzha district administration and the Local Self Government Department , the lake 's surface area has shrunk mainly due to land encroachment . Citing previous studies , the report notes that the surface area of the lake diminished by 27% between 1917 and 1990 . The drastic reduction in not only area , but also depth , has significantly reduced the lake 's floodwater retention capacity and impaired its critical ecosystem services , including water purification , biodiversity support , and sediment transport . The unchecked proliferation of water hyacinths has further worsened the situation , contributing to dangerously high levels of chemical oxygen demand and biological oxygen demand . As a result , the fish catch has declined by about 66% over the last three decades . <p> The efforts to rejuvenate the lake are being spearheaded by Alappuzha District Collector Alex Varghese . The initiative draws " inspiration from the Namami Gange Programme " . It gained momentum on October 28 , 2024 when a workshop was held focusing on addressing the challenges of restoring the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ water resources , tourism , biodiversity , environment and sanitation , disaster management and climate change , and revenue -- were constituted . A ? 188.25 crore comprehensive five-year plan was formulated and recently submitted to Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan . The estimate may be revised based on the detailed study on water resources and irrigation projects being conducted by the Centre for Water Resources Development and Management . <p> The short-term goals include the removal of plastic waste , construction of bio-shields to protect farmlands , fish ranching , weed eradication , and the construction of 31 bio bunds , each 1 km long in 31 grama panchayats . The long-term targets include dredging the lake bed to increase its water-holding capacity , promoting organic farming to prevent pollution from pesticides and chemicals , conserving the flora and fauna , establishing sewage and faecal sludge treatment plants in flood-prone Kuttanad , manufacturing value-added products from water hyacinth , and boosting tourism and fish yield . <p> While the report is under the State government 's consideration , 28.72 tonnes of plastic waste and a greater quantity of water hyacinth @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ conducted under the aegis of the Alappuzha district administration . <p> Rejuvenating the lake is critical for enhancing the region 's resilience to climate change impacts such as erratic rainfall , sea-level rise , and intensified flooding events . However , it is easier said than done . For instance , houseboats are among the top sources of pollution in the lake . While the report calls for enacting strict laws against unauthorised vessels , previous efforts to rein in illegal houseboat operations have been largely ineffective . Another significant hurdle is land encroachment . The expert committee report notes that reclaiming encroached areas " necessitates strong political support and decisive action . " Since Kuttanad is part of the Vembanad wetland ecosystem , the lake 's restoration should be linked to the revival of the entire Kuttanad region . <p> Coordinated collaboration among various stakeholders , including local communities , district administrations , and different levels of governance , will be key to overcoming these complex challenges and will require support from the Union and State governments . <h> Comments <p> Comments have to be in English , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ personal . Immediate triggers , such as medical emergencies , religious ceremonies , dowries , food shortages , or the sudden loss of a job or a breadwinner , may force an impoverished worker to seek a loan or advance from an employer or labour agent . However , deeper systemic issues amplify this vulnerability : discrimination and social exclusion based on religion , ethnicity , or caste ; widespread illiteracy and a lack of access to information ; employer monopolies over local financial and labour markets ; and the dominance of social elites . These elements transform a simple economic transaction between lender and borrower into a mechanism of social control and exploitation . <h> Policy and plan <p> India had abolished bonded labour in 1975 . To meet the 2030 target of eradicating bonded labour , around 11 lakh individuals would need to have been rescued annually since 2021 . Given that only 12,000 bonded labourers were rescued between 2016 and 2021 , expecting lakhs to be freed annually is overly optimistic . <p> In addition to bonded labour , crores of unorganised Indian workers , particularly migrants , endure forced labour in India , which closely resembles bonded labour . According to a National Sample Survey Organization of India report , the country 's total employment across the organised and unorganised sectors was approximately 47 crore . Interviews with hundreds of workers -- mostly migrants forced from their villages by climate change , crippling poverty , and a lack of job opportunities -- lay bare a system rigged against them . These workers lack stable wages , facing meagre pay , precarious conditions , and the constant threat of dismissal . This exploitation , a deliberate assault on their dignity , is perpetuated by a system prioritising profit over people , ignoring modern-day slavery . @@124176960 <p> Stumps of Sitka spruce , drowned from subsidence during an earthquake at a subduction zone some 1,600 years ago , in Neskowin , Ore . <p> Marli Miller/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images <p> Scary headlines about the Pacific Northwest sinking into the sea are circulating online , with warnings that a major earthquake in the notorious Cascadia subduction zone could be worse than expected . <p> What 's behind this new alarm ? Fortunately , research has not uncovered a new risk that Seattle will become the Lost City of Atlantis . Instead scientists have examined the combined effects of two well-known phenomena : sea-level rise from climate change and the likely consequences of a major earthquake in the region . It was already known that sea level along the coast of northern California , Oregon and Washington State is estimated to rise by 1.3 to 2.9 feet by 2100 because of a warming climate . It was also well known that a magnitude 8 or higher earthquake in the area could cause the coastline to slump by up to 6.5 feet . What the new study , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Academy of Sciences USA , adds is an understanding of how much additional land would end up being at a high risk of flooding because of these two combined threats . <h> Why Does Sea-Level Rise Matter ? <h> On supporting science journalism <p> If you 're enjoying this article , consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today . <p> While the East Coast is already seeing the effects of beach erosion and rising sea levels , the Pacific Northwest ( PNW ) has been protected by its geology -- so far . The coast that extends from northern California to Vancouver Island in British Columbia sits on a subduction zone where the Juan de Fuca , Explorer and Gorda oceanic plates slip beneath the North American continental plate -- parts of the ever moving slabs of rock that make up our planet . Right now the fault system is quiet , meaning it has not had a large earthquake for more than 300 years , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of an inch each year . This geological uplift , a consequence of the interactions of the tectonic plates , outpaces sea-level rise in many areas , so the PNW has been relatively shielded from effects such as extreme flooding events or coastal erosion . <p> But over the past 7,000 years or so , at least 11 major earthquakes have struck the Cascadia region where these faults reside . The last of these temblors occurred in 1700 , and geologists can still see evidence of it causing the coastline to drop between 1.6 and 6.5 feet in the blink of an eye . " We have these really rooted organic soils that are suddenly overlain by this really clean tidal mud , indicating they were suddenly dropped down and were buried and basically converted to tidal flats , " says Tina Dura , a coastal geologist at Virginia Tech and first author of the new study . <p> What no one had really studied , Dura says , was the combined effect of this sudden subsidence and the slower inundation caused by sea-level rise . <h> How Much of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ her colleagues looked at earthquake scenarios that would yield different ranges of subsidence , from 1.6 to 6.5 feet . They also compared such an earthquake 's effects at today 's sea levels with those at sea levels forecasted for 2100 . By that time , sea-level rise is expected to outpace the geological uplift of the PNW and may reach as much as 2.9 feet . <p> The team found that if an earthquake that caused more than six feet of subsidence were to happen today , the 100-year floodplain in estuaries in Cascadia would expand by 115 square miles . Were this quake to happen in the year 2100 , with the additional pressures of sea-level rise , those estuaries would expand by 145 square miles . That would be triple the flood-prone area that is seen today . <h> How Worried Should We Be ? <p> In the event of a magnitude 8 quake in Cascadia , subsidence would not be the first issue on anyone 's mind . A large undersea quake could cause a devastating tsunami that would immediately threaten lives and structures . The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of elevation of the current 100-year floodplain , Dura says , and the earthquake-driven tsunami could be more than 30 feet high . <p> A good comparison might be the 2004 Sumatra earthquake and tsunami that killed more than 227,000 people around the Indian Ocean or the 2011 T&amp;omacr ; hoku earthquake and tsunami that killed more than 16,000 in Japan . Both caused subsidence , but the severity of the initial disaster far eclipsed concerns about coastal slump . <p> Understanding the subsidence is important for preparation , however , Dura says . Municipal planners may want to avoid building new electrical substations or wastewater treatment plants in the areas that could become floodplains . ( A 100-year floodplain has a 1 percent chance of flooding each year . ) Tide- or storm-driven flooding of low-lying bridges , roadways and airports in the immediate aftermath of the quake could affect evacuation efforts and rescue attempts . And many people may find that property that was once safe from flooding is now regularly inundated , particularly in built-up areas such as Seaside , Ore. , Gearhart , Ore. , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> " The tsunami is a process that takes minutes to hours after the earthquake , " she says , " whereas , once the tsunami recedes , we 're still going to have the land level that has dropped down and changed the floodplain footprint .
